8RPK5KwYhgA.tx: 10 out of 10 dentists agree that you should brush twice and floss once every day. But what if you just... didn’t? What would happen if you stopped doing any oral hygiene? And how long would it take for your mouth to get messy? Let’s start with the last day you do brush and floss. This routine doesn't actually clean your mouth completely. Rather, you’re maintaining a delicate balance between hundreds of microbial species. At any given time, most of these microorganisms fit into one of two groups: commensals and pathobionts. High quantities of commensals are good for oral health. They minimize inflammation, protect our mouths from harmful foreign microbes, and produce ammonia, which neutralizes tooth-decaying acids. Meanwhile, an abundance of pathobionts is bad for oral health. Sugar-eating varieties produce acid that damages the mouths’ tissues, and meat-eating varieties thrive on the debris inflammation creates. Thorough brushing and flossing remove members of both groups, but commensals can proliferate faster, so they tend to bounce back quicker. This means daily oral hygiene keeps your commensal population higher than your pathobiont population. Most oral disease is the result of this balance being disrupted, and that happens pretty quickly once you stop brushing and flossing. For the first 72 hours, the most notable side effect is supremely bad breath. But by day four, hordes of pathobionts have coated most of your teeth in a sticky film called dental plaque. Over the following days, the plaque triggers an immune response that causes your gums to bleed and inflame— an uncomfortable condition known as gingivitis. After a month, your booming pathobiont population may be releasing enough acid byproducts to break down enamel and begin causing cavities. But the bigger problem is that your pathobionts far outnumber your commensals. Since both microbe communities grow at an exponential rate, even if you started brushing again, pathobionts would always have a numerical advantage. Researchers are investigating ways to add commensals back into the microbiome, but currently there’s no way to remodel a mouth that’s been overcome by pathobionts. In this new world order, pathobionts divide and conquer. Some pump out acids that dissolve the minerals in your teeth and drive dental decay, making them sensitive to pressure and temperature. Others lead the gums to swell and recede, creating gaps that get colonized by yet more plaque. Over the following months, this cycle breaks down the gum’s soft tissues, advancing your gingivitis into first stage periodontitis— a painful infection of the gums. This loose gum tissue feeds the meat-eating pathobionts, perpetuating their cycle of destruction. But the food you add to this environment also has a huge impact. The more sugar a diet contains, the more acid-producing pathobionts it supports— all of which release destructive waste that further inhibits the growth of commensals. After roughly a year without brushing, your gums have been inflamed so long that the body’s immune response starts impacting the underlying bone. This process, called alveolar bone resorption, makes the jawbone recede and weakens the scaffolding holding your teeth, leaving them to wobble and fall out. This kind of tooth and bone damage is permanent, but tooth loss isn't the end of this unhygienic journey. In this advanced stage of periodontitis, areas of injured tissue have formed below the gum line that give pathobionts access to your bloodstream. From here, these bacteria can worsen health conditions throughout the body, including cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, diabetes, and arthritis. In some cases, they can even exacerbate neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s and accelerate the growth of malignant tumors. Thankfully, there’s a simple way to avoid this grim outcome. If you picked up these tools 2 or 3 weeks into our unhygienic experiment, you could have fully reversed the early stages of gingivitis and tooth decay and avoided all the permanent damage that followed. Better yet, brushing with even coverage for two minutes at a time will help your teeth make the most of your toothpaste’s fluoride, which replaces some of your exposed enamel with acid-resistant fluorine atoms. So remember, brushing for two minutes twice a day will keep the pathobionts at bay.

a_4eFB8pPwI.tx: You're about to buy some bargain bin headphones when you spot a real bargain. This pair is more expensive, but it's selling for half its usual price. Surely this is the better buy, right? It’s possible! However, it’s also possible you’re falling for a psychological trick retailers use to influence what you buy and what you’re willing to pay. From the late 1800s, economic theory often assumed that consumers were rational actors who pursued the optimal financial choice. But while consumers are reasonably rational on average, they’re also vulnerable to impulse purchases, savvy salespeople, and other external factors that make them, well, irrational. 20th century psychologists investigating these factors learned that human decision making is rarely perfectly logical. And by the 1970s, this research informed the birth of behavioral economics, a new field exploring the intersection of economics and psychology. Behavioral economics operated off a new assumption, introduced by economic sciences laureate Herbert Simon. His model, called “bounded rationality,” argued that consumers have limited information, limited time, and various psychological constraints that lead them not to the optimal financial choice, but simply one they feel good about. So how do we decide what's good enough? Rather than using logic, behavioral economists say we fall back on heuristics— mental shortcuts for making decisions easier and faster. For example, the anchoring heuristic suggests that the first piece of information you get becomes your baseline for future decision making. So if a menu's first item costs $50, you'll compare other prices against that reference point. Psychologists like Daniel Kahneman thought heuristics predict many consumer choices— which means they can be manipulated to control them. Case in point, while those discounted headphones might be 50% off, it’s also possible the original price was inflated to begin with. Anchoring is just one of many heuristics retailers exploit. Consider this: which of these cleaning products would you buy? How about now? Both are equally effective and basically cost the same, but careful language and pricing makes one more appealing. This is the framing effect, and it’s one of several psychological phenomena that short circuit our ability to assign value. Here’s an example of another: some American grocery stores tried encouraging customers to bring reusable shopping bags by offering a 5 cent credit. But this proved less effective than charging a 5 cent fee for using disposable bags. In other words, the desire to avoid losing 5 cents was more motivating than gaining 5 cents. This is called loss aversion, and retailers trigger this fear of losing value by emphasizing a sale’s scarcity or looming deadline. All these tactics suggest our perception of value is more important than what something is actually worth. And that effect goes deeper than you might think. In a 2008 study, subjects were put into MRI machines and treated to samples from five bottles of increasingly expensive wine. Participants reported preferring the expensive samples, and MRI images confirmed this claim. But in reality they only tasted three bottles, with the two cheapest pulling double duty as the two priciest. Of course, retailers don’t just manipulate your perception, they control the spaces you shop. Supermarkets often place high-margin items at eye level and design stores to guide you past them. Behavioral economist Richard Thaler and legal scholar Cass Sunstein call this subtle product placement “nudge theory,” and it works online as well. Sites might nudge you by suggesting related items to purchase or by pre-selecting add-ons. So if retailers are boxing you in, what can you do about it? First, shop slower. Heuristic-based decision making is quick and instinctive, so slowing down to run the numbers can pull back the curtain on a flashy deal. Deciding what a product is worth to you before shopping can help set your own anchors. And always ask yourself why you want this deal. Buying something just because it’s a bargain means you might not be in control of your choice. Above all, remember that retailers and advertisers aren’t just selling products— they’re designing your choices. And once you understand the psychology behind their designs, you might gain something even more valuable than a discount: the ability to choose on your own terms.

NPJ9KZqrl50.tx: In 1740, while Swiss naturalist Abraham Trembley was tutoring the sons of a nobleman, he had scooped up some pond water for them to study when he found something shocking inside. He couldn't identify the odd little thing or even tell if it was a plant or an animal. Its way of moving and consuming things seemed animal-like. But when he cut parts off, or even split it in two, it regenerated, which was decidedly plant-like, in keeping with its green hue. Trembley noted the organism’s similarity to the Hydra, the monster from Greek mythology, and the name stuck. Today, we know hydras are animals capable of some incredible feats, apparently including immortality. They comprise a genus of tiny aquatic animals in the broader phylum Cnidaria. Some cnidarians, like jellyfish, have a stationary polyp phase, then a free-swimming Medusa stage. But hydras and some of their relatives stay polyps their whole lives. Hydras have relatively simple cylindrical body plans, one end forming the foot, the other the mouth, framed by fanning tentacles. They’ll eat just about any critter they can snag. And although they can scoot around if needed, most of the time, they remain stuck to things using a gluey substance secreted from their foot. They can reproduce sexually, but they more often do so asexually, budding new growths off their bodies. Where exactly they hunker down in the freshwater ponds and slow-moving streams they populate varies by species, which likewise differ in shape, size, and hue. Green hydras, for one, bask in sunny spots to feed the photosynthetic algae they host, which lend them their color and provide sugars in return for other nutrients. This explains some of Trembley’s “animal-or-plant” confusion. Meanwhile, other species, like brown hydras, stick to the shade and hunt more actively. Hydra tentacles are covered with stinging cells containing little capsules of pressurized, harpoon-like structures. When triggered, they fly out at explosive speeds, immobilizing small prey. This adaptation doesn’t protect hydras from larger predators— but what they lack in defenses, they make up for in their unparalleled regenerative abilities. Not only can hydras regrow lost appendages, they can also reassemble themselves after going through a blending process of sorts, where they're completely broken down into individual cells. To do this, these cells first aggregate into a sphere, then they begin to sort themselves, gradually hollowing out and elongating as they group into external and internal layers. Soon, one end sprouts a few buds, which become the tentacles, while the other end develops into the foot. In a matter of days, the hydra is back in one piece, bopping around and catching worms like nothing happened. In labs, this process has helped shed light on embryonic development, because some of the stages and proteins are common among all animals— though the ability to perform it willy-nilly, as hydras do, is decidedly not. K1s2lv4cpw0.tx: In this English lesson, I want to teach you some phrases we use to express disbelief. Phrases we use when someone tells us something and we don't quite believe them. Let's say Jen said to me, "Bob, you won't believe this. I bought a lottery ticket and we won two million dollars." I might say one of two phrases. I might say, "Shut up." Now, that's normally a phrase we use rudely to tell someone to stop talking, but we also sometimes use it in a funny way to express disbelief, or I might say "get out," which means exactly the same thing. I'm simply saying to Jen, "I don't really believe you, … really believe you." So those are your first two phrases. You may have heard these phrases if you've ever watched the TV show Seinfeld. Elaine often shoves the other characters and yells "get out," as an expression of disbelief. And I think once or twice she even shoves and says "shut up." Basically meaning she doesn't believe what the other person is saying. The second phrase I want to teach you that we use to express disbelief is the phrase "you did not." Let's say I've always wanted to go to a Taylor Swift concert, but I can't really afford the tickets. If Jen said to me, "Bob, I got a … Swift concert," I might express disbelief by saying, "You did not." Basically, I'm saying to Jen. I don't believe that you actually got the tickets. You did not get the tickets, and I express it with that phrase: "You did not." And then I would probably follow up by saying, "Did you really?" So another expression of disbelief that you can use when someone tells you something that's hard to believe, you could simply say, "You did not." The third phrase we sometimes use to express disbelief is the phrase "Stop it." Imagine that Jen and I are going on a trip. We have tickets to go on an … " The airline just texted, and they've upgraded us to first class for free. I might reply and say, "Stop it." Basically, what I'm saying is, "I don't believe you." And if that did happen in real life, I wouldn't believe Jen, and I would actually say that. I would say, "Stop it! I don't believe you. Show me the text." So, another phrase we sometimes use to express disbelief: "Stop it." The fourth phrase that I wanted to teach you today that we use to express disbelief is actually two phrases, and it's the phrase "Are you serious?" or just the word "Seriously"? Let's imagine a friend of yours … prestigious job, and you don't think they're going to get it. If they call you or text you and say "Hey, I got the job," you could respond by saying "Are you serious?" or "Seriously?" basically expressing a little bit of doubt that what they're telling you is actually true. But at the same time, I think you're sort of believing them. So, when someone tells you something cool and exciting, that's another way you can respond. You can say "Seriously?", or you can say, "Are you serious?" The fifth phrase that I wanted to teach you that we use to express disbelief is the phrase "For real?" This … phrase, maybe not slang, but certainly very informal. And here's an example when I would use this phrase. If someone told me today that the United States and Canada have come to an agreement on free trade, I would say "For real?", because I would certainly be doubting that that has happened. If you don't know, Canada and the US, we're having a little trouble coming to an agreement about how we trade things across the border. But certainly, if someone said, "Did you read the news? They've signed a new free trade agreement." I would say "For real?", because I certainly would be doubting that … amount of disbelief. The sixth phrase I wanted to teach you today is the phrase "You're joking!" or you can also say "You're kidding!" and we would use this again to express disbelief. cqDZt0BOlBI.tx: In 1940, a Royal Airforce pilot named Gordon “Mouse” Cleaver was battling with a German fighter plane when his aircraft was hit by cannon fire. The canopy of his plane shattered in battle, and he had no choice but to flip upside down, fall out, and parachute to safety. This left shards of the plane's canopy embedded in his face and eyes, which is why fighter pilots usually wear protective goggles during their flights. In his rush to get ready that morning, Cleaver had forgotten to bring his protective goggles with him. Now getting shrapnel in your eyes isn’t great, but there was a silver … flying one of the most legendary fighter planes of World War II called a Hawker Hurricane. When you think of a fighter plane, you probably think of a frame like this And then you might imagine an armored glass canopy for the pilot to see out of. But it turns out, glass is actually NOT a great material for things that need to fly. Glass canopies are heavy, stiff, and when they break, they shatter into thousands of tiny pieces that get in literally everything. Which is why, beginning around World War II, aircraft designers started using acrylic. Acrylic is the common name for Poly-methyl … glass in fighter planes because it’s lightweight and flexible. A lighter plane gets better fuel efficiency, while a more flexible plane is better at absorbing stress. The biggest advantage though, is how it shatters. When an acrylic canopy breaks, it does so in larger, more blunt fragments, instead of the thousands of tiny shards. And, that’s MUCH easier to remove from the bodies of injured soldiers. When Cleaver had all that shrapnel in his eyes, that shrapnel was shards of acrylic. And, he had to undergo more than a dozen surgeries to remove it. The surgeons never were able to get all of … seem to be causing any of that. There was no noticeable inflammatory reaction. Not only that, but Cleaver still had pretty good vision for the severity of his injury, despite having shards of a foreign material in his eye. That gave Dr. Ridley an idea. This is your eye. It sits inside your orbit, the protective bony socket in your skull, and it’s also surrounded and controlled by six extra-ocular muscles. That’s what allows us to move our eyes around. Then there’s your cornea, your iris, the lens, and finally your retina, which converts all the information from the rest of the eye into … your pupil, controlling the light as it passes through to reach the lens, retina, and the optic nerve. This ability to change focus is one of the most important functions of your eyes. Think about how you have to refocus the lens on a camera or microscope every time you change the zoom. This is happening in your eye … the lens and the cornea work together to serve this function. Your cornea does most of the heavy lifting, but your lens can literally change shape to change your focus. This is what allows us to see things that are close up, or really far away, and our lens does this so … to age 80 will get cataracts. It causes blurred vision, brightness sensitivity, seeing colors less vividly, and a whole host of other symptoms. Cataracts are the leading cause of blindness globally, and for a long time, we really didn’t have a good way to treat them. We tried, though. Back in 500BCE, doctors tried a method called couching. This comes from a french word that means “to put to bed” or “to lay it down” because that’s what they were essentially trying to do with the cataract. The way they tried to accomplish this was by taking a sharp needle, shoving it in the patient's eyes, … But it also meant the lens couldn’t serve any of its normal functions because it’s in the side of their eye. You’re not really supposed to have a lens at the side of your eye, and, shockingly, people didn’t react well to having part of their eye shoved aside with a giant needle. Having a part of the eye where it didn’t belong, combined with the lack of disinfected needles at the time, almost always resulted in infections, and eventually blindness after the procedure was done. Another technique we tried was called extraction, and it's just what it sounds like. They cut a large incision in … behind, and infection was still a pretty big problem. Then came phaco-emulsification... In this procedure, they STILL inserted a needle into your eye, but then ultrasonic waves broke up the lens into tiny pieces and those got sucked out. Can we stop putting needles in people’s eyes? The smaller incision for this approach, plus improved infection control by the 60s when it came around, made removing a cloudy lens much safer. There was still one issue though … you were left without a lens. Which brings us back to Dr. Ridley’s idea. When he saw how well Cleaver’s eye responded to the … exact same shape as the original lens. This is called the intraocular lens, or IOL, and it works something like this: A surgeon makes tiny incisions near the edge of your cornea, and inserts an instrument to break the lens into smaller pieces. Sometimes the lens will be softened with a laser to make it easier to remove. Once that’s complete, a new, flexible artificial lens made of acrylic is inserted in its place. When they were first invented, IOLs were actually considered pretty controversial because eye doctors only ever really took things OUT of people's eyes, they weren’t supposed to … of the implants. But as the technology improved, IOLs became standard for treating cataracts. An IOL is able to focus light before it comes into your retina pretty similarly to how your natural lens would, and you can even get customized ones! Some IOLs now have blue light filters, UV filters, or they can help fix astigmatism. Today, 20 million cataract surgeries using IOLS are performed every year. And in 1987, Gordon Cleaver himself was diagnosed with cataracts. He got an IOL, and regained his vision. All thanks to the surgery inspired by him forgetting his goggles all those decades ago.

QmxiqRYLTd0.tx: This is a 2008 Mercedes-McLaren SLR Roadster and it's an incredibly special supercar that I think is way underrated. This car is really rare, it's really fast, it has a cool history between two awesome automakers and it drives a lot better than most people think. It's also full of quirks and features and today I'm going to review the SLR and show you everything. Before I get started, big news. So, … comes to kind of a pointy front end at the very front of the car. And that was intended to mimic the look of a Formula 1 race car because this was done in partnership with McLaren and Mercedes-Benz, the Formula 1 buddies. l29K-ZkARmE.tx: Troy’s princess, Cassandra, wasn’t cruel to her soon-to-be sister-in-law, the legendary beauty Helen, out of spite. It was because she was suffering under the weight of a tortuously twisted curse, which haunted her with appalling visions linked to Helen’s arrival. Helen was already married to the Spartan king Menelaus, after all. And when Cassandra’s brother, Prince Paris, prepared to sail to Sparta, she foresaw his calamitous attachment to Helen and begged him to stay. But he’d merely dismissed her, fallen for Helen, and returned to Troy with her in tow. Beset by violent premonitions, Cassandra then warned that Menelaus’ vengeful crusade would lead to the brutal fall of their family and the city of Troy. But once again, people ignored her. In fact, they always did. And this was the crux of her curse. As a young woman she had been pursued by the god Apollo. He offered her the gift of prophecy. But when she withdrew from his advances, he twisted his gift into a maddening hex: from that day on, Cassandra would be able to precisely see and describe the future— but her prophecies would never be believed. Despite this, Cassandra resolved to always speak the truth, even as her family fell deeper into denial. Her dire warnings became increasingly repellent to her father, Trojan King Priam. And when the war began, as she’d predicted, he declared that her meddling was bad for morale and confined her to a high tower. From this unobstructed lookout, Cassandra watched everything unfold. Over 10 agonizing years, she witnessed her own grisly visions of senseless destruction come to pass on the battlefield below. When dawn broke one day to reveal a huge wooden horse in place of the Greek encampment, the Trojans believed that the victory had finally been secured. Their enemies appeared to have fled, leaving this inscrutable token of peace behind. But as others streamed into the streets to celebrate, Cassandra realized the insidious truth. Brandishing a battle-axe and a flaming torch, she descended from the tower and ran at the wooden horse, alerting everyone that it was a trick. Instead of heeding Cassandra’s warnings, they wrestled her to the ground and scoffed that she was getting more paranoid with age, then proceeded to tug the behemoth gift horse inside the city’s walls. As Troy fell into an oblivious slumber that night, Greek soldiers descended from the wooden horse's belly. All had gone according to plan, and they scattered among the city streets, intoxicated with their victory, to unleash a torrent of pent up, violent chaos. Cassandra had seen her city burn and heard her people’s screams many times, but that didn't make the reality any easier to bear. Her nightmare had come to pass. As dawn neared, the commander of the Greek army, Agamemnon himself, arrived to claim Cassandra as his prize. He dragged her back to his ship, boasting relentlessly of his victory as they set sail. But Cassandra told him plainly that he'd be punished. Earlier in the years of battle, Agamemnon had sacrificed his daughter to the war effort, hoping the gods would favor the Greeks in return. Now Cassandra saw that his wife, Clytemnestra, awaited his return, poised for revenge. But just as certainly as she saw that Agamemnon was sailing towards his own murder, Cassandra saw that she would also be killed in the fallout. As always, she confronted the grim fate. In her lonely pact with the truth, no matter how ugly, Cassandra had always stood apart. After all, was it not her but everyone else who had fallen victim to the curse, living in deceit’s shadow, oblivious to reality until the bitter end?

2A1IEBFt6Xg.tx: To coincide with the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, Japan launched the world’s first high-speed train, the Shinkansen. Capable of running at 210 kph, this groundbreaking bullet train inspired countries around the world to invest in high-speed rail. Today, these trains regularly travel at over 300 kph, on par with the takeoff speed of a commercial airplane. But could these trains go even faster, whisking passengers to their destinations quicker than the smoothest flight? To answer this, it helps to understand how these trains reach their already impressive speeds. There are three main factors that separate bullet trains from traditional, low-speed trains: engines, aerodynamics, and infrastructure. Most traditional trains are powered by combustion engines, which combust fuel— typically diesel— to turn an electric generator. This electricity is then used to power motors that turn the train’s wheels. High-speed trains, on the other hand, use electric engines to power their motors. This process is more energy efficient than combustion and allows train operators to reach top speeds more quickly. Next up is aerodynamics. While low- and high-speed trains use the same steel wheels to minimize friction with the track, bullet trains are also designed with aerodynamic bodies that slice through air with minimal resistance. Engineers could use these slicker designs on traditional train cars. But while upgrading to electric engines would make low-speed trains more efficient, they wouldn't get much benefit from these aerodynamic designs because of the third factor: infrastructure. Traditional train tracks were built to meet people where they lived, ensuring stations were accessible to any potential passengers. But to prevent derailments in these highly populated areas, trains need to frequently decelerate to safely hit turns and cross roads. High-speed rails, on the other hand, were built to prioritize speed. They run on long, straight lines that avoid road crossings, sharp curves, and high traffic areas. These three differences allow high-speed trains to reach top speeds over double their traditional counterparts. And since their infrastructure allows them to travel longer distances between stops, they spend more time cruising near top speed, often traveling up to three times the average speed of traditional trains. But new technology is emerging to make even faster trains. To eliminate friction between rails and wheels, engineers have developed new magnetic levitation, or maglev, trains. There are two major approaches here. In electromagnetic suspension, magnetized arms wrap under the track and pull the train up. Meanwhile, in electrodynamic suspension, coils embedded in the track create a pattern of alternating magnetic fields that interact with magnets on the train to float the vehicle a few centimeters in the air. To change speed, train operators alternate the direction of the trains’ magnetic field, attracting the front of the train to the next coil to speed up or reversing the field’s phase to brake. Given enough runway, these trains can reach speeds from 430 to a theoretical 600 kph, allowing them to make the over 4,400 kilometer trip from New York City to Los Angeles in as little as seven hours. So why haven’t we built maglev trains, or even high-speed trains, everywhere? First, these trains require lots of energy, most of which is needed to overcome air resistance. In fact, at 300 kph, this task accounts for over 80% of a train’s energy consumption. Engineers are researching ways to reduce air resistance, such as putting maglevs in near-vacuum environments. But building a vacuum-sealed tunnel across an entire country would be an infrastructure project of science fictional proportions. Besides, it’s hard enough to build regular high-speed rails. To go fast, trains need long, straight tracks with wide curves, which are very difficult to build in mountains, cities, or densely populated areas. Building such routes is costly, politically sensitive, and often physically impossible. Despite these hurdles, Japan and China are expanding their existing high-speed and maglev rails, and several projects currently in development might finally bring high-speed rail to the US. But we’ll need to carefully consider our trains’ top speeds alongside cost, energy use, and safety to keep the future of train travel on the right track.

4FEkQRcE3cs.tx: Today's question is: Can stories help you learn English? Imagine this: you’re sitting by a fire, listening to someone tell a story. You’re pulled in by the characters, the suspense, the emotions. You’re not thinking about grammar rules. You’re not repeating vocabulary lists in your head. You’re simply *immersed*. Now—what if I told you this is one of the most powerful ways to learn English? In this episode, we’re going to talk about learning English through stories: what it looks like, why it works, what to watch out for, and how you can use it every day to move closer to fluency. So what does learning a language through story look like? Learning through story isn’t just watching movies in English or listening to podcasts and hoping some words stick. It’s about using stories—narratives with characters, problems, and resolutions—as your main source of language input. That could mean reading a *graded reader*, which is a book written at a certain language level. It could mean listening to a podcast that tells personal stories, like *The Moth*. It could mean watching a TV show with a strong narrative—something where you’re following characters over time. The important thing is this: stories aren’t random. They have structure and context. And that structure helps you understand and remember the language much more deeply than isolated words or grammar drills ever could. So why do stories work so well? First, **comprehension in context**. When you meet a new word inside a story, you often guess the meaning from what’s happening. You don’t need a dictionary every time. Do you know how many words I know the meaning of but couldn’t exactly explain the meaning to you? But I can use it in a sentence correctly? That’s the power of learning in context. Second, **memory boost**. Neuroscience tells us our brains are wired for stories. We remember narratives far better than disconnected facts. If you learn the word “forest” inside a fairy tale where a character gets lost in the forest, you’ll remember it. Third, **motivation**. Stories are fun. When you’re curious about what happens next, you naturally stay engaged longer than if you were staring at a vocabulary list. And finally, **real-world fluency**. Stories show language the way it’s actually used—idioms, natural grammar, cultural references—all packaged in a way that’s alive. Think about how children learn their first language: bedtime stories, cartoons, daily conversations. They don’t study a “word of the day.” They grow up surrounded by stories. But—let’s be real—there are some challenges. If the story is way too difficult, it can feel overwhelming. You might spend more time looking up words than actually enjoying the story. That’s exhausting and discouraging. On the other hand, if you only enjoy the story passively, without noticing the language, you might not learn much at all. And sometimes, cultural references in stories can be confusing if you don’t share the same background knowledge. That’s why finding the *right level* of story is so important. Stephen Krashen, a famous linguist, calls this *comprehensible input*. The idea is simple: your learning should be just above your current level—what he calls “i + 1.” Here’s a simple test: - If you need to stop every sentence to check the dictionary, it’s too hard. - If you understand every single word without effort, it might be too easy. - The sweet spot is when you understand most of it, but you also notice a few new words or structures. That balance keeps you challenged without burning you out. Now, let’s talk about two different ways to approach stories: **intensive reading** and **extensive reading**. Intensive reading means studying a short text very carefully. You look at vocabulary, grammar, and structure in detail. This builds accuracy and depth. Extensive reading, on the other hand, means reading a lot for pleasure without stopping too often. This builds fluency, speed, and comfort with the language. Think of it like exercise: intensive reading is lifting weights—slow, focused, powerful. Extensive reading is jogging—steady, enjoyable, good for stamina. Both are valuable. The key is to balance them. So how can you start using stories in your own English learning? - Begin with **graded readers** or short stories at your level. Don’t jump straight into Shakespeare or modern novels unless you feel ready. - Try **story podcasts**. For example, *The Moth*. Many come with transcripts. - Check out *The Fable Cottage* for fairytales you might already know in your native language. - Watch TV shows with strong narratives, with subtitles at first. - Check out Olly Richards’s Short Stories collection in English. It’s designed for language learners by language learners. - Keep a **story journal**. After reading or listening, retell the story in your own words—out loud or in writing. This helps you process the language actively. - Most importantly: be consistent. Even 10 minutes a day builds up over weeks and months. Remember: fluency doesn’t come from memorizing lists. It comes from living in the language. And stories let you live in English. Let’s recap: stories give you context, memory, motivation, and fluency. But you need to choose the right level, balance intensive and extensive reading, and keep at it consistently. So here’s my challenge for you: this week, pick one short story in English. Read it or listen to it. Don’t worry about being perfect—just immerse yourself. Notice a few new words, enjoy the narrative, and let the story do its work. Because every story you read in English brings you one step closer to thinking, dreaming, and living in English. Thanks for listening! Until next time! Bye!

QIqKGMM8ivM.tx: When scientists sample the soil, bodies of water, or even the air for DNA, they routinely unmask thousands of tiny mysteries— unique fragments of fungal DNA that don't match any known species. This DNA belongs to cryptic organisms, often referred to as “dark fungi,” which, like dark matter and dark energy, are simultaneously all around us and yet elude discovery. Scientists estimate that somewhere between 2 and 12 million species of fungi remain undiscovered— their physical structures yet to be seen, either because they’re microscopic, live hidden within other species, or for other unknown reasons. The diverse fungal kingdom, which includes everything from baker's yeast to edible mushrooms to foot infections, has long defied assumptions. For centuries, biologists mistakenly classified them as plants, for what they’d argue were good reasons: many grow from the soil atop branching, root-like networks. But at the biological level, they're very different. Unlike plants that harness energy from the Sun, fungi eat by decomposing matter or siphoning nutrients from other organisms. Rather than cellulose, their cell walls are made of chitin, the same material in exoskeletons of insects, like beetles, and crustaceans, like shrimps. Fungi are actually more closely related to animals than plants, sharing a common ancestor which first appeared over 1 billion years ago. Over time, fungi evolved to occupy a range of ecological roles, including intertwined relationships with plants. Many plants can't survive without these fungal partners. Ectomycorrhizal fungi envelop plant roots, trading nutrients they forage in the soil, like phosphorus and nitrogen, for carbon to fuel their growth. Another guild, called arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, goes so far as puncturing plant root cells like straws to aid in this exchange. This relationship enabled plants to colonize land 470 million years ago, when nutrients were far more difficult to obtain from the barren, rocky ground. Other fungi evolved remarkable strategies to defend against, exploit, and manipulate their neighbors, often by producing an arsenal of compounds like antibiotics, toxins, and even psychedelics. Many mushrooms in the genus Psilocybe produce psilocybin, a molecule that binds to serotonin receptors in the bodies and brains of animals. This causes hallucinogenic effects in humans, though psilocybin likely evolved to deter hungry slugs or snails. Clathrus archeri, a cluster of red tentacle-like mushrooms, sometimes called “devil’s fingers,” emits a sticky, spore-filled slime called gleba. It smells like rotting flesh, attracting nearby flies that feed on it and carry spores away on their bodies. Other fungi take a more extreme approach. Many species of Cordyceps infect ants, chemically hijacking their nervous systems with toxins and connecting directly to muscle fibers to puppeteer their movements. The infected ants become zombies, compelled to climb to high places and eject millions of fungal spores. Still other fungi are more self-reliant, carving out solitary lives in extreme environments, like the walls of nuclear wastelands. Researchers have observed at least 37 species of fungi living among the ruins in Chernobyl, home to one of the world’s worst nuclear disasters. Many are rich in melanin, a pigment that can absorb harmful radiation to protect fungal cells and DNA. But some don’t just endure radiation— they eat it. Studies conducted on the International Space Station revealed that species like Cryptococcus neoformans can convert absorbed gamma radiation into useful energy, establishing a previously unknown metabolic strategy, and redefining the perceived limits of life. The planet-wide consequences of this fleet of fungal functions are still making themselves known. In the Arctic tundra, fungi form a vast underground network, helping plants survive the harsh winters, while stockpiling carbon from the atmosphere. Scientists suspect these soils may be particularly rich in rare, dark fungi. And these fungal networks, along the plants they support, may sequester about 1 trillion metric tons of carbon— 10 times more than the entire Amazon rainforest— potentially keeping Earth resilient against climate change. The fungal world we see is vast and wild. Who knows what other wonders might be growing just beyond our view.

6hCo4S_1Fhw.tx: In February 2012, pro skier Elyse Saugstad was carving through the slopes of the Cascade Mountains when a crack formed in the snowpack above her. Before she was fully engulfed by a 5,000-ton wall of snow, Elyse heard “AVALANCHE!” just in time to react with a lifesaving maneuver. So, how could she survive this crushing snow surge? Avalanches are the rapid descension of snow, ice, rock, or a combination of these down a slope. They can be destructive natural disasters and personal tragedies: in the United States alone, avalanches kill an average of 27 people annually. These alpine nightmares don’t just awaken out of nowhere; they need three specific conditions. First, the mountain needs to have the right slope, typically between 30 and 45 degrees. This is shallow enough to allow snow to build up on the slope, yet steep enough to provide enough potential energy for movement. Second, they typically need a layer of sturdy snow deposited over a weak or unstable layer, or what’s sometimes called “something over nothing.” Take the Cascade Mountain avalanche, where recent heavy storms deposited a nearly 1-meter-deep slab of fresh snow. Below this sat a thin layer of surface hoar. These are delicate, feathery ice crystals that form when water vapor in the air rapidly freezes on the surface of snow, almost like dew in the wintertime. Finally, avalanches need a trigger, something to collapse the weak layer and put the snow in motion. A trigger can be natural, such as heavy snowfall, strong winds, rainfall, or even other avalanches. Or they can be human-caused, like the surface impact of skiers or snowmobilers. Since fractures can propagate quickly through the snowpack, triggers can originate hundreds of meters away— upstream, downstream, or even adjacent to the avalanche’s path. Once in motion, how quickly an avalanche moves depends on the slope’s steepness, its exposure or vegetation cover, terrain roughness, and the type and amount of snow involved. For example, dry, light, and loosely bonded snow tends to travel fast, forming a powder cloud as it moves. In contrast, wet snow avalanches, caused by water moving through the snowpack, travel more slowly but are much denser and can be particularly destructive. Larger avalanches can travel more than 160 kilometers per hour, breaking trees, destroying buildings, and burying roadways. In 1970, one particularly massive avalanche consisting of 50 to 100 million cubic meters of glacial ice, snow, mud, and rock reached speeds of over 300 kilometers per hour. This avalanche proved to be the deadliest in history, engulfing an entire Peruvian town and killing 18,000 people. Avalanches aren't always this large, but even smaller ones can be dangerous for anyone caught in their path. As snow rushes downhill, it can behave like both a solid and a liquid, making its movement difficult to predict. At the fastest-moving front, surface snow moves faster than the snow beneath, pulling victims deep into the snowpack and scattering them across wide areas, making rescue difficult. Once an avalanche slows, the snow loses its fluid-like properties and compacts, leaving victims immobilized and unable to escape on their own. For these reasons, the best way to survive an avalanche is to avoid one altogether. Thankfully, at most ski resorts, parks, and even highways, avalanche workers mitigate risk by continuously monitoring the weather, stability of the snowpack, and human activity. If a threat is detected, they'll close terrain and may even intentionally trigger a controlled avalanche with explosives or artillery. However, there are regions where avalanche risk is not actively mitigated, known as the backcountry. Here, you are responsible for managing your own risk. Local avalanche centers provide avalanche forecasts, and anyone entering the backcountry should understand them, be properly trained, and carry essential rescue gear. And ultimately, in high-hazard terrain, there's no way to completely eliminate risk. The group at the Cascade Mountains consisted of highly experienced skiers. Yet the area was very exposed, and following a large storm, the avalanche danger forecast was elevated. In the end, three skiers lost their lives. But not Elyse, as she was able to deploy an inflatable airbag. These devices are imperfect and a last line of defense, yet can keep a victim closer to the surface, improving their chance of rescue should disaster strike.

wsstlwuE5XY.tx: For those of us who are worried about climate change, it's no doubt challenging times. It feels like the end of the light of the tunnel gets further as companies and governments pull back. And I get it. It's hard to feel motivated with headlines like these. But that is not the full story. In reality, a shift towards a climate solution-based economy is already underway. Not just because it protects the climate, but because it's becoming more profitable, more practical and more affordable. Despite all the setbacks, we will solve this problem. However, we have to be strategic. We cannot solve … climate problem at once. We have to identify the systems that can unlock many others. The places where one smart move can create ripple effects across the entire economy. One of the most strategic, most powerful, but also most overlooked of those systems is shipping. If shipping was a country, it would be the sixth largest greenhouse gas emitter in the world. Many of these ships aren't just powered by fossil fuels, they're built with fossil fuels, and they transport fossil fuels. Maritime shipping is a climate problem on three fronts. One, for the cargo it carries. Crude oil and gas account … roughly one third of maritime trade. Around half of natural gas is shipped in a liquefied form called LNG, and LNG trade has doubled during the past decade. Two, because of the fuel ships burn. Most ships still burn heavy fuel oils or increasingly, LNG, which releases carbon dioxide and methane, a dirty superpollutant that accelerates climate change and air pollution. Three, because of the steel ships are made of. Most steel is made using dirty coal. Steel production is responsible for another 8% of global emissions. So shipping is not a side issue in the climate crisis. It is one of the … hidden levers in the entire climate fight, a system if pulled the right way, which can unlock a faster energy transition. It's tempting to think of oceans as diffused and decentralized, but when it comes to ships, their supply chains converge in one place: East Asia. South Korea in particular dominates global shipbuilding, steel production for ships and the public finance behind them. And we are now at a critical moment, with Asia as a key leverage point. The world has experienced how volatile fossil fuels are with the war in Ukraine. Again, we are experiencing the same with the war in … Middle East. Right now, East Asian economies are making a decision. Do we keep funding fossil fuels or pivot towards offshore wind installation vessels, green ammonia tankers or ships made with clean steel? Because clean options don't scale just because they exist, they scale when policy, finance and regulation align to make clean attractive. My organization, Solutions for Our Climate, works to do just that. And we're no beginner here. We've done it before with coal. From behind-the-scenes international negotiations to grassroots communities, from courtrooms to hilarious videos portraying … climate facts, we know what message to put in front of who, how and when. Our work actually contributed to ending coal financing by the East Asian coal giants. (Applause) And now we're ready to take on shipping the same way. First, we expose emissions, policy gaps, financial risks. Take LNG transportation. Global LNG trade depends entirely on ships. Each LNG carrier ship costs 250 million dollars, takes three years to build and locks in decades of emissions. The system is surprisingly concentrated. 70 percent of these ships are built in one country, South Korea. In 2022 alone, in one year, … Korean government banks provided more than 10 billion dollars of financing for these ships. The technologies around these ships are monopolized by a handful of companies. So this isn't just a business story. It's a political and financial choke point. Second, we redirect capital and governments away from fossil expansion. If we cut the financing of these ships, we will limit LNG expansion. Our aim is simple. Make LNG a no-investment zone. (Applause) We're asking private banks to end the financing of these ships. We're pushing Asian lenders to adopt exclusion policies. Third, we build … demands and rules for clean alternatives. The technology for clean steel or green shipping fuels is already here. What's missing is the supply chains and demand to meet it. Our push for finance, regulations and infrastructure will change this. That means building clean fuel supply chains, creating new demand through green shipping corridors between ports. Over time, renewable-rich regions will replace oil refineries as shipping fuel production hubs. We apply the same approach for clean steel. Green hydrogen will replace the role coal served in steelmaking. This isn't just aspirational. The … is already underway. We've already convinced four European banks to exit from a major LNG project in Mozambique. We've blocked new coal-based steel investments. We've secured financial support for hydrogen-based steel mills. We're doing the work and building the momentum. And now we will supercharge it through Navigate to Clean, a new initiative to clean up maritime shipping. With the generous support of the community of Audacious donors, we will turn shipping from a conduit of dirty trade to a driver of clean trade. We are a team of marketers, diplomats, lawyers, shipping experts. We're … organization with global reach. We know the system and how to move it. We've done it with coal and we can do it with shipping. It is difficult times, yes, but with the right strategy and leverage, we can eliminate up to 2.2 gigatons of emissions per year by 2032. RCNO3k4QL5M.tx: Four months ago, my house was raided by the agents of the Venezuelan regime. They destroyed the walls, the ceilings and even killed my dogs. After that, they decided to take away my Venezuelan nationality, something that is prohibited by the Venezuelan Constitution. What sparked this was a public statement I made supporting the law enforcement and military buildup against Nicolás Maduro that led to his capture on January 3. And maybe the fact that my house was only blocks away from Delcy Rodríguez’s, interim dictator of Venezuela. For my family and I, the journey of persecution has been very … years. In solitary confinement, the sound I remember most is not screaming. It's the locks. One lock, then another, then another. Nine locks in total. I was in complete confinement, so locks became very present to me, and they became the framework through which I started to think about freedom, which was the reason I was in prison. Please tell your wife to find my wife." And in that way, we developed a protocol to communicate within prison. It took time, a lot of iterations. And for 12 hours, we took complete control of that prison. After that, things became even more lonely and more difficult. I … and finally I crossed a river and went into Colombia. And I began exile. We were very different -- skin color, religion, languages -- but we were very similar in our struggle for freedom. So we decided to create the World Liberty Congress, which has become the largest global alliance of freedom fighters and democracy defenders. 60 countries are represented -- (Applause) 60 countries represented in the World Liberty Congress. And that gave me … and doctors to get a $100 monthly support. But we had a problem. The financial system was taken by the regime. It was surveilled by the regime. So we turned to stablecoins and Bitcoin, and we were able to support more than 70,000 medical doctors and nurses without the intermediation of the regime. The problem was very clear. The problem was the gatekeeper. Whenever there is a gatekeeper, there is a problem. It doesn't matter if the gatekeeper is a government, if it's a bank, if it's a company. So what we need to figure out is how we can … agent, and I am working with other people for them in their autocratic countries to have their own agent that is completely sovereign. But keys are hard to master. I remember when I was in prison, waking up to an assault rifle pointed my head. And several men in the cell just tearing everything apart. I was very scared. uBwkMc1llmM.tx: In the late 560s, a Germanic group known as the Lombards was wreaking havoc through northern Italy. To escape the invaders, boatloads of people fled into the Venetian Lagoon, a morass of swampy mudflats and scattered islands. Formed over centuries by the outflow of silt from the Po and Piave Rivers and the counterforce of Adriatic currents, this marshy maze was constantly shifting and disappearing. These qualities made it both the perfect spot to hide and a very unstable place to live. So the new arrivals set out to tame the lagoon and build the most unlikely of cities from the mud. While some fishermen already inhabited the region in stilted huts, the settlers wanted to build a foundation to support heavier, longer lasting structures. Little did they know, their work would support Venice to this very day. They drove clusters of 1 to 3-meter-long wooden piles into the ground, in a process that squeezed out groundwater and compacted mud around the piles. This created an oxygen-free environment that protected the wood from insects and fungi. The piles were still vulnerable to minor bacterial damage, but otherwise impervious to rot. And this sealed system of wood, water, and mud is still supporting Venice 1,500 years later. Wooden beams and stone platforms above the piles provided the bases for buildings. And sometime around 697, the settlers formally declared their new home the Republic of Venice. Initially, footbridges were built to connect the islands, but these were prone to decay, collapse, and fire. Many, like the famed Rialto Bridge, had to be regularly rebuilt, each time incorporating new materials and techniques to improve their longevity. By the 11th century, the channels between islands had been reinforced into stone-lined canals navigated by slender gondolas. And unlike the rest of Europe, where nobles typically rode above commoners, the city's layout necessitated foot travel for all classes. Yet despite this clever engineering, the Republic still had no land for farming, so Venetians were heavily dependent on trade. Fortunately, Venice's location made it the perfect port city to connect markets from Europe to the Silk Road. Its canal network allowed boats to dock close to warehouses, and the challenge of navigating its narrow waterways protected the city from outsiders. These advantages helped make Venice a major maritime power, and the 1200s began with their biggest business deal yet. The Pope brokered an arrangement with Venice’s elected leader, Enrico Dandolo, to produce ships and arms for the Fourth Crusade’s anticipated 33,000 soldiers. Dandolo agreed, investing huge amounts of the republic’s money and resources. But when it was time to set sail, only one-third of the soldiers arrived, with less than half of the promised payment. Furious, Dandolo redirected the crusading army against Venice’s Christian rivals, including Constantinople. This campaign laid the foundation for Venice's overseas empire, and over the following centuries, Venetian merchants like Marco Polo ventured as far as China. During the Renaissance, the republic became a hub of art and intellectual life. Its sail-making looms were repurposed to create vast canvases, its craftsmen pioneered various printing techniques, and the silica-rich sands from the Ticino and Adige rivers fueled extravagant glassworks. However, in addition to art, silks, and spices, the Venetians also traded enslaved peoples to work in private homes or on ships. Once freed, some stayed in the city, even finding work as gondoliers. Venice's dominance over the Mediterranean remained unchallenged until the mid-15th century, when the Ottomans conquered Constantinople. In the following centuries, the Ottomans used their navy to interfere with Venice's business, all while new transoceanic trade routes excluded Venetians. The republic soldiered on until French attacks forced it to dissolve in 1797, at which point Venice traded hands between Austria and France several times before finally being ceded to Italy in 1866. No longer able to compete commercially, Venice was reinvented as a tourist destination. But today, rising sea levels are threatening to sink the so-called “floating city.” In 1900, the then 900-year-old Basilica di San Marco flooded about seven times a year— now it experiences roughly 250 annual floods. And tourists are perhaps just as dangerous. As millions of annual visitors speed along in motorboats, they erode the muddy barrier protecting Venice’s foundations. Left unaddressed, these modern advances could destroy one of the world’s most remarkable cities.

on1L_jblaw8.tx: We all have a fundamental desire to be seen and understood. And to have other people see us the way we see ourselves: capable, competent, intelligent, playful, charismatic -- you get to choose the adjectives that fit you. But that's why when there's a disconnect, when we feel misjudged, it can be very disconcerting, even painful. Several years ago, when I was teaching at Stanford, one of my students, Lauren, came to me for help unraveling some confusing feedback she'd received at her new job. Lauren said of herself that she was painfully shy and timid, especially around new people, so she was … of the beholder. But I've spent 25 years studying nonverbal communication, researching the predominant cues that we as human beings use to assess credibility, confidence, leadership presence. And the bottom line is that there are ground rules, metrics. Certain behaviors lead to very predictable assessments on the part of the listener. So if you can better understand what behaviors lead to what types of assessments, you can just be more in charge of the image that you project. Which means that if I look at you, both my nose and eyes point directly toward you. And if I look at you, eyes and nose directly toward you. Notice what happens right now when my eyes and nose move a little bit more independently. I'm very likely to look uncomfortable. But I could also look sneaky. Or mischievous. Or judgmental. (Laughter) Where if, at level four, I was really making a connection with you, at level … measure, so they just think they're talking far louder than they are. And this is a very common problem, but I experienced a pretty extreme case of this in one of my seminars. Eugene was frustrated that his ideas were not being acknowledged in meetings. He'd bring up a point that he thought was pretty important, but receive no reaction. In giving him feedback, I asked him if he was aware that his volume was significantly soft, a level two or below on my scale, and that I was missing about 50 percent of everything he was saying. He looked up at the other participants and he said, "Is … you could identify the specific behavior that needed to be addressed, it might be relatively easy to fix. So, for example, so far in this conversation, I have been trying to follow the guideline of keeping my head and shoulders level. She started in a very small, asymmetrical posture, eyes cast down, and she had a tendency to speak with a thin voice, using upward inflections. So I started by asking her to stand with her weight balanced over both feet and her shoulders level. And she did. Then I asked her to pick up her gaze so that her head was level. And she did. But I don't believe being authentic means you in your raw state, or you not trying very hard or not caring what other people think. My definition of authenticity is when the adjectives you would use to describe yourself are the very same adjectives someone else would use to describe you. There's alignment. But if you see yourself one way, and let's just say that's brimming with potential and ready to take on more responsibility, but other people are not seeing that about you, changing your behaviors so that they would see that about you, that's not … to swallow, no one, including me, is immune to a blind spot. One day, many years ago, I played with my children in the morning and then I took them off to preschool. And that day, as I went around running all of my errands, everyone I came upon greeted me with these big beaming smiles. It’s like magic dust had been sprinkled over the Earth and everybody was in a fantastic mood. But they seemed especially happy to see me. When I got home, I caught a glimpse of myself in the mirror, and I had forgotten that when I was playing with the children in the morning, I drawn a kitty nose and … this brings me to my call to action. Be courageous. Seek out outside feedback. Intentionally get an outside view of yourself. Even if it's on your cell phone, in your living room. Because the good news is that qualities like leadership presence, credibility, confidence, these are not special talents that some people have and some don't. These are skills. Skills that any one of you can develop. (Applause)

35jnupIq4Jw.tx: Today’s episode is not a lesson, although you will learn plenty of new vocabulary. Today I’m telling you about a little…situation I had to deal with last week. It’s a storytime! There are three things in this world that are almost universally hated: jury duty, the DMV, and the post office. Perhaps these are only part of American culture, but I think a version of all of these exist in most countries. I’ll explain each one, then I’m going to tell you which one I had to deal with this past week. So, jury duty. What is that? It’s a mandatory responsibility of citizens to serve as part of a jury … A jury is a group of people who listen to each side of the argument and the jury renders a verdict. A verdict is a decision, saying guilty or not guilty. When we talk about verdict, we often use the verb “to render” which basically means to deliver or give. A jury renders a verdict. Specifically, a jury of your peers. A peer is someone who is more or less equal to you in society, not just a bunch of rich people or a bunch of lawyers or anything like that. The jury is selected randomly from the eligible citizens in your local area and then there’s a selection process, lots of … So in this case, DMV is an acronym that stands for Department of Motor Vehicles. The DMV is responsible for administering–meaning, giving–motor vehicle registrations and driver’s licenses. Literally everyone I’ve ever met hates going to the DMV. It’s so universally hated, in fact, that there’s a joke about it in the Disney movie Zootopia. If you’ve seen Zootopia, do you remember the scene where Judy and Nick go to the DMV? Judy is in a big hurry and she’s shocked to see that all the workers at the DMV are sloths. This is some clever commentary about how people view the DMV. The third … expression in America: going postal. I don’t want to describe it here, because the origin is very sad and violent, but it is related to the post office and if you’re curious, you can look it up on your own. So, I had to go to the post office last week. Let me explain why. I ordered some books. To be precise, I ordered six books and they were being delivered in two packages: four books in one package and two books in the other. Well, I was super excited for these books, so I was psyched when I checked the tracking information and saw an update that my packages were out for delivery. … asked my husband to check the mail when he got home later that afternoon. One of my packages arrived! One, but not both. I was so confused because they should have arrived together, at the same time. Well, later there was an update to the tracking status. It said “delivered”! But it also said “individual picked up at postal facility.” That sounds like a person picked up my package at the post office. A regular person, not a worker, because it said “delivered.” I was so confused. What did this mean? Did someone else have my package? Did the post office give my package to someone else? Was my … this phrase from the tracking update: individual picked up at postal facility. I ended up on Reddit. If you don’t already know, Reddit is an online forum where you can post questions or comment about every topic imaginable and it can all be completely anonymous. There was a Reddit post about this exact topic. It seemed that this was a fairly common problem that had happened to a lot of people. Many of the people actually got their packages in the end even though they had to wait a little bit sometimes. So I had a little bit of hope. I decided to go to the post office in person. I thought … in, there were already eight people in line! Eight! And of course there was only one worker. It was a sad place. It’s an old building. Everything was old and dirty. It smelled a little weird. I didn’t want to touch anything. It felt like a prison. Well, the one good thing was that the worker was actually really nice! I showed her the tracking information on my phone and explained that the status—individual picked up at postal facility—was strange because no one in my household picked it up. She said that it was likely a computer error. She also said that it actually happens quite often … I went home. I taught a class. I waited some more. I checked again at three o’clock. And it was there! It was actually finally there! I had the books in my hands. I practically skipped back to my house, I was so happy. Probably you wouldn’t be as happy as I was about these books, unless you’re really interested in languages. If you’re curious, the books I got are: The Etymologicon by Mark Forsyth. Etymology is the study of word origins. This book starts with a particular word, explains the origin, and then connects it to another word, explaining the origin of that word, and connecting it … Invention by Silvia Ferrara. This book is about writing. Specifically the invention of various writing systems all over the world. I don’t know much about language from a writing point of view and I know this book will teach me a lot about that topic. I also got Other Wordly by Yee-Lum Mak. This is a collection of words and expressions specific to their native languages. For example, to tartle. This is a Scots word that means “to hesitate while introducing or meeting someone because you have forgotten their name.” We don’t have a word for this in English. It’s beautifully illustrated and … by Deborah Cameron. This is a book exploring if men and women speak differently. This is one of the first books I’ve come across exploring language from the point of view of gender, so I’m really looking forward to learning more. So those are all the books I got and the little drama that surrounded their arrival. I went to the post office and lived to tell the tale. When you live to tell the tale, it means you survived the event you were talking about. Thank you for joining me for this little storytime. I hope you enjoyed it. nmaew6zJDZI.tx: Hello, hello, my friends! How are you all today? I hope you’re doing well. In this video, I am going to talk about me— specifically, me as a teacher: what my classes are like and also why I teach the way I do. I’ve been teaching since 2019. As of now, as of filming this video, that’s five and a half years. That’s crazy, bro! Here’s what I’ve learned from being a teacher and how it changed how I teach. #1 - Not demonizing mistakes “To demonize” something means to label something or treat something as really bad, even evil. I could also use the word “stigmatize” here. “To stigmatize” something means to label something very negatively. For example, school stigmatizes mistakes. If you make too many mistakes, you are punished for it. Schools treat mistakes as the worst thing you can make. But if you think about how people learn, you know that mistakes are part of the process. In fact, mistakes equal progress. You cannot do anything perfectly the first time. So in my classes, I am very relaxed about mistakes. The first phrase I teach my students is: nit picky. “Nit picky” describes someone who cares way too much about tiny little details, especially mistakes. I am not nit picky. This means that I’m not the best teacher for everyone. Some students *want* a very nit picky teacher, and that’s okay. That’s personal preference. I am not nit picky for a variety of reasons. First of all, I value—I care about—communication above all. If I understand your message, then communication was successful. That’s my number one priority: successful communication. Because that’s what language is: communication. Second of all, I do not want to stop you every time you make a mistake. Stopping you when you make a mistake stops the flow of the conversation, so the conversation is less natural. I teach conversation classes, so the goal is to have natural conversations. Third of all, there’s research that suggests that instant correction is not the most effective method in conversation. Instant correction is better for things like grammar exercises. But in conversation, instant correction may not be the best method. So how *do* I correct mistakes? I make notes about mistakes and during a natural pause in the conversation, I will talk to my student about that mistake. I focus on patterns of mistakes. If I hear you make the same type of mistake many times, I want to talk about that. I think this is more effective, because then you can make one change and it has a broad effect. If I don’t understand what you’re saying, I will make a confused face, like this, and we will figure out your meaning together, and I will make corrections then. But usually, I make a note, and then we talk about it later. #2 - Comfort is king When we say that “{something} is king” it means that that thing is top. I most often hear this expression to say, “Cash is king” although that is probably not true anymore. But in my classes, I want my students to be comfortable. I want my classes to be fun and relaxed. If the student is stressed, anxious, or worried, it makes learning more difficult. There’s actually a name for this: the Affective Filter Hypothesis. This Hypothesis says that when a student’s negative emotions—such as stress, fear, embarrassment, or anxiety—when those negative emotions are high, it becomes significantly, significantly more difficult for learning to happen. I know this from personal experience. The language classes I took in high school were *awful*. I was *so* stressed, *so* anxious, and I was not able to learn very well at all. So based on my experience as a student, and based on the Affective Filter Hypothesis, my goal as a teacher is clear: My goal is to create a fun, safe, relaxed environment for my students. When students are relaxed and happy, they learn more, they learn better, and they learn faster. Finally, #3 - the value of taking notes When I first started teaching, I wrote my notes by hand. The notes were just for me. But then, early in my teaching journey, I was also learning French and I took a class with a French tutor and this tutor used a Google Doc to share notes with me, including corrections. I thought that was great! So I started to do the same. Every class, I create a Google Doc, share my screen, and then type notes during our conversation. It’s really useful to do it this way, because then both of us can see what’s happening. I don’t just write mistakes and corrections, I also write example sentences, include links to other resources, pictures, etc. At the end of class, I send my student this document, so they can reference it if they like. Or do nothing with it! That’s also personal preference. So those are three things like I to do as a teacher, and why I do them. If you’re still watching, leave me a comment with a pencil emoji so I know you’re one of my loyal viewers. Also, if you have had an English teacher in the past, what techniques did your English teacher use that you liked? I would like to know. Thanks for watching, friends! Until next time! Bye! qtwVVVvwIWg.tx: Hello, hello! Today we are going to talk about what is holding you back. You're working hard, but you feel stuck. Like there's some invisible wall between where you are and where you want to be. Well, you're not alone. As an English teacher, I've seen so many students face the same challenges. Today, I want to talk about three common barriers that might be holding you back— and more importantly, how to break through them. Remember, learning a language is about growing, connecting, and making English part of your everyday life. Let’s get started. #1 The Perfectionism Trap The first barrier is what I call "the perfectionism trap." Have you thought: "I can't speak until my grammar is perfect." "I'm embarrassed because I make too many mistakes." "I need to know more vocabulary before having conversations." "I should understand everything before I speak." If you have had thoughts like these, you might be stuck in a perfectionism trap. Perfectionism is like trying to learn how to swim without getting wet. It's impossible! Language isn't about perfection—it's about communication. Language is art. When you focus too much on making zero mistakes, you end up not practicing at all. And without practice, how can you improve? Native speakers make mistakes all the time. They use incorrect grammar, forget words, and mispronounce things. But they keep talking, and so should you! To overcome this trap, here’s what I recommend: Remember that mistakes are your teachers. Let mistakes teach you something about how you think about the language. Give yourself 5 minutes to not worry about making mistakes. Just talk, just communicate. After 5 minutes, try another 5 minutes. Keep going. Remember: mistakes are feedback, not failures. #2: The Isolation Island The second barrier is what I call "the isolation island." This is when you think: "I'll practice English when I travel abroad someday." "I don't have anyone to practice with." "I can only learn English in class or from textbooks." "Real English is too difficult for me right now." If you have thoughts like this, you might be stuck on an isolation island. Isolation means to be separate from, like to be alone. Language is a social act. When you isolate your English learning from your real life, you're cutting off opportunities to learn. Textbooks and classes are helpful, but they're just the beginning. The good news is that English is everywhere! Even if you don't live in an English-speaking country, you can bring English into your everyday life. Choose one of your hobbies or interests and explore it in English. Love cooking? Watch cooking videos in English. Passionate about sports? Follow athletes on social media who post in English. Create small daily habits: five minutes of writing in English, talking to yourself while doing chores, or describing what you see on your way to work. Change your phone language to English. If you can find a language partner online, even better. Remember: Language thrives in connection. The more you connect English to things you genuinely care about, the more naturally you'll absorb it. #3: The Comparison Trap The third barrier is "the comparison trap." This is when you think: "That other student speaks so much better than me." "I've been studying for years and I'm still not fluent." "My progress is too slow compared to others." "I should be at a higher level by now." If you think like this, you’re probably stuck in the comparison trap. This is a terrible place to be; I know the feeling. Comparing yourself to someone else never gives you an accurate picture. Everyone has different backgrounds, different amounts of time to practice, and different learning styles. When you focus on comparing yourself to others, it can destroy your motivation and joy in learning. The only person you should compare yourself to is who you were yesterday. If you track your progress— for example, write in English every day— you can look back three months ago and you can see your progress. Set personal, achievable goals based on your life situation. Maybe it's understanding your favorite TV show without subtitles, or being able to talk about your job in English, or reading a specific book. Celebrate small wins. Did you understand a joke in English? Did you have a short conversation with a tourist? Did you figure out the words to a song you never understood before? These are real achievements! Remember: Your language journey is uniquely yours. Progress isn't linear—it comes in waves. Trust the process and keep going. But here's what I want you to remember: You can break through all of these barriers. Learning a language isn't about being perfect, it's about connecting with others and expressing yourself. It's not about studying in isolation; it’s about bringing English into your everyday life. And it's definitely not about comparing yourself to others; it’s about celebrating your own unique progress. If you are ready to break through a barrier, leave a muscle emoji in the comments. Thank you for watching! Until next time! Bye!
