29naHEtQayg.tx: I’ve been thinking about this question a lot lately: How long does it take to learn a language? I have a couple of thoughts on this, and I know you’ve probably thought about this too, so let’s talk about it. How long does it **really** take to learn English? My main thought about this is: it depends. Not everyone’s favorite answer, I know. Here’s what I think it depends **on**: It depends on what you want to do with the language It depends on how different your target language is from your native language It depends on the time you have available It depends on the resources you have available It depends on if you’ve already learned a foreign language before So let’s take these point by point. First, what you want to do with the language. If you want to reach complete mastery of the language, it will take you more time than if you just wanted to travel comfortably in that language. Do you want or need to become fluent? Or do you want to just be able to have conversations? This will change how much time it will take you. Second, how different your target language is from your native language. I’ll be honest. I don’t believe there is a “hardest language in the world.” I think we all perceive a language as more or less difficult if it is very similar to or very different from our native language. For example, the Foreign Service Institute has sorted a bunch of different languages by their difficulty for a native English speaker. If the language was very similar to English—such as Spanish and other Romance languages—then it was a category 1 language: it would not require an enormous amount of time for a native English speaker to learn. But for languages that are very different from English—like Mandarin Chinese or Japanese or Korean—it will take much much longer to learn. Now I want to talk about these numbers. These numbers bother me a bit. I understand these numbers come from over 70 years of professional research and expertise. However, these numbers are an **average** and represent **class hours** and let’s be honest: the classes at the FSI are probably much higher quality than a university class. So I think this number is not very useful for the average learner because you are probably not learning a language at the Foreign Service Institute. You are probably learning English at home with an app or a course, and maybe not with a professional teacher either. Therefore, this number is not going to match your situation and I don’t think you should take this number seriously. That brings me to my third point: the time you have available. Let’s be honest: we want more time than we have. You are probably trying to learn English while having a job and having a family. Even if you did have a lot of time in your day, it is very difficult to spend a lot of time—many many hours every day—studying English in a focused way. It’s exhausting! Maybe you can do this one day or two days or maybe even three, but can you do it every day for five or six months? Probably not and that’s OK. But it’s important to make English part of your everyday life. So think about how much time you **can** spend focusing on English: 10 minutes, 20 minutes, 30 minutes? Whatever the number is, make that your goal. For example, I can spend 20 minutes during lunch to study Spanish. I can do that five days a week, so that is my goal. Watch a Spanish video five days a week during lunch. That brings me to my fourth point: the resources you have available. The resources you should use depends on the goal you have. For example, if your goal is to have conversations in English, then most of the resources you use should focus on listening and speaking. A textbook, for example, might not help you so much if your goal is to have conversations. However, if your goal is to study at an English speaking university, then using a textbook might be more helpful for you because you need to do more than have conversations. Probably your goal is to have conversations in English with native speakers. In that case, I recommend listening as much as possible. If you only have 10 minutes in your day to study English then listen for 10 minutes. My final point is: if you have already learned a foreign language, then learning a second foreign language will probably be a little bit easier for you. So you can see why there is not an easy answer to this question. But that’s actually a good thing because it means you can go at your own speed. You don’t need to compare your speed and your progress with other people’s speed, other people’s progress. Remember: comparison is the thief of joy. And language learning is very personal. I hope you will not feel bad about your learning speed. If you do feel bad I hope you will take that time you want to spend feeling bad and use it for studying English. Because I know you can do this. I know you might feel doubt, but if you have good habits, if you practice English a little bit every day you will learn. Thanks for watching. Until next time! Bye!

MClIzIOAn_U.tx: If you're young and visiting the UK, or you're a student planning to study in the UK, one of the things that you might want to experience is our nightclubs. There are plenty of pubs and bars where alcohol is served, but nightclubs are the places that are open later and which also have dance floors. You can dance, there may even be a DJ. Nightclubs or clubs, CLUB, are up until quite late at night or even early morning you might say. But rather like the crisis that Britain is facing with pubs, where lots of pubs close every week, the same seems to be happening to our nightclubs too. Where is … too. And nightclubs were certainly around and popular when I was young enough to go to them, and especially when I was a student. Even after the age of 30, I would sometimes go out with my work friends dancing on a Thursday night, because it was fun. No longer, I'm afraid. My days of clubbing are over. But nightclubs have been operating for a long time, and for my generation, going to a nightclub was a rite of passage. There's a phrase. A 'rite of passage' - that's R-I-T-E. It's an event that marks an important change in your life, like moving from being a child to an adult. Suddenly, being … together at a rave, dancing under a light show until the sun came up. Never my thing, but you may be familiar with that. But over a third, 33% of these places, rave venues, have closed since the pandemic, since 2020. So today, we're asking a big question. Have the British forgotten how to party? Sometimes what we're famous for in a negative way. And yes, 'to party' can be used as a verb. Or is it just possible that we are finding other ways to enjoy ourselves? And the theme of our nightclubs closing, this has been picked up by lots of writers online. There are articles like 'The End of … called 'Hedonism'. Other BBC articles focus slightly differently with titles like, 'Are sports clubs replacing nightclubs for socialising?' So instead of going out drinking and dancing to meet new people, today socialising means turning up to run or do sport. That's the more popular way to meet people. rj-G_gmFWtE.tx: I have a hot take: I really like transmission towers. Sure, a lot of people hate them, and some people even actively campaign against them. And to be fair, they are kind of obtrusive on the landscape. But so much of our modern life is hidden behind shiny enclosures or abstracted away from us without a single hint on the outside about what’s happening on the inside. Electrical transmission lines are the opposite. They’re out in the open for anyone to have a look - a constant reminder of what it takes to power the world… They’ve just been this way in so many places for so long that now they … they carry distribution-level voltage, somewhere between 10 and 15 kilovolts, but sometimes up to 35 kV. This is generally classified as medium voltage, or you’ll sometimes just hear it referred to as primary voltage, especially by distribution linesworkers to distinguish it from the lower, secondary voltage that connects to building service panels. An electric arc usually requires about 20 to 30 kV per centimeter to jump an air gap, so you actually don’t need much clearance at all around medium voltage conductors to avoid the issue. That’s why the insulators that support overhead … towers and sewage lift stations, but that’s another video. Just because of the sheer scale of distribution infrastructure, these poles are relatively standardized. Most of these parts can be picked up from a catalog without a lot of detailed engineering involved. Many utilities develop their own standards and maintain relationships with equipment distributors, so the engineers can put together designs quickly, crews know how to maintain and swap equipment, and so on. When we level up to the transmission side, that changes a lot. You don’t just buy transmission towers "off the rack.” To move … go up quicker, and are often less expensive than the alternatives, but you actually don’t see them used very often. They’re mostly limited to very remote, unpopulated, flat areas where the main bottleneck for construction is transportation. The relatively lightweight tower sections are easier to move, even if you have to use a helicopter. The problem is that they take up a lot of space. Acquiring the land below a transmission line, called the right-of-way, is one of the most expensive and legally complex parts of a transmission project. Of course there are a lot of technical and engineering … They’re still pretty lightweight, using a trusswork of small steel members. But they’re strong enough to withstand all the forces required without needing guys. And they come in a practically endless variety of shapes. For single circuit lines, the phases can be spaced horizontally along a cross arm; or they can be held in a triangle on what’s often called a delta tower. Many transmission lines carry two circuits, which means six energized conductors. Plus almost all transmission towers have one or two static lines above the energized lines to intercept lightning strikes and … a few in North America, particularly in the Ohio River Valley, Appalachia, and Quebec. At a quick glance, all the towers along a transmission line may look the same, but they’re almost always not. That’s because different parts of the line have different structural demands. A tangent or suspension tower is the simplest. This is a tower supporting a relatively straight part of the line. The conductors come in and leave in the same direction, so the lateral forces are balanced. It’s just weight and wind to withstand, so these towers are usually the lightest ones. You can tell them apart from … lines can kind of clutter up what might otherwise be a pristine view of the countryside. Personally, I like the look of latticed steel, but there is an alternative that many people prefer: the tubular monopole. With a single, self-supporting column, I guess they are a little sleeker and less industrial-chic. But the benefits aren’t just in looks. They also have a tiny footprint, perfect for congested areas where land costs or environmental constraints demand as narrow a right-of-way as possible. Also, with a single foundation (as opposed to the two for H-frames or four for lattice towers), … an interesting thing, at least it is to me. I usually think of a power or current rating to be some hidden limit that was meticulously calculated or tested for a particular device. For transmission line conductors, it’s a lot simpler than that. Even though they usually look ‘saggy’, transmission lines are under quite a bit of tension. Like all metals, when they get hot, they expand, and they sag even more. So, the current limit is really just how hot they can get before they sag down too low to maintain adequate clearance from the trees and the ground. Of course, with more current you get … of it. But reconductoring is only one of the many examples of how we just keep innovating, making it easier to balance the factors that drive these projects. With so many constraints in play, it’s almost impossible to put anything into a category on the grid. There’s so much variety. 1IVlILdETAw.tx: You open your fridge to grab a snack and recoil at the scene before you. Strawberries coated in fuzz, green islands floating on your yogurt, and bread growing a patchy, white beard. But as your stomach growls, a question pops into your head: surely you could eat around these masses of mold, right? Molds are a diverse group of fungi containing hundreds of thousands of species, only a fraction of which have been identified. They're also everywhere. Mold spores are all around you, constantly drifting through the air in search of the right landing place. Specifically, they’re looking for a particular combination of temperature, moisture, and nutrients, most often found in soil, plants, and food. This makes the produce aisle one of their favorite spots to settle down. After landing, they sprout a tube that becomes a network of branches called hyphae. These sprawl out through the food, releasing enzymes that break down their new host into easily digestible fats, sugars, and amino acids. As the mold spreads, it builds structures that make and release fresh spores to start the cycle all over again. Most food molds complete this process in 1 to 3 days, but the exact timeline varies from mold to mold. And differences between hosts determine what species can take root in the first place. Every food has a specific mix of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals that make it compatible with different molds. For example, berries’ high moisture and sugar levels suit the needs of Botrytis cinerea, Penicillium, and Cladosporium which are often found on berry plants, fruits, and nearby soil. Acidic foods like tomatoes are commonly colonized by Alternaria alternata, which have pumps in their cell walls that push acid out of their systems. And bread is beloved by Rhizopus stolonifer. This mold is well-suited to the food’s high starch content, which it breaks down with the help of a specialized enzyme. Whatever mold a food attracts, it doesn't just grow on the surface. Like most fungi, mold develops a root-like structure called mycelium, that spreads deep into the host. This is why food safety experts recommend tossing moldy items altogether, since removing visible mold doesn't get rid of the mycelium inside. Even if you use high temperatures to kill a mold’s body, its spores can still survive— going dormant until the conditions are right to resurface. And while cold can kill some molds, others can survive subzero temperatures. The cold generally slows their growth, so putting produce in the fridge can stretch its lifespan for a few extra days. But other molds thrive in the damp darkness of a condensation-filled crisper. So if moldy food is unavoidable, is it at least edible? Well, molds exist in a spectrum from harmful to helpful, and the so-called spoilage molds on your aging groceries are mostly harmless. They can trigger allergic reactions like any other food, and eating large quantities can cause vomiting and diarrhea. But for most people, accidentally taking a bite of something moldy won’t make them seriously sick. And they’re unlikely to take a second bite since mold tastes bad. Our sense of taste likely evolved as a survival mechanism, helping early humans identify tasty, nutritious food and avoid deadly toxins. In fact, this same evolutionary trait might be why some do enjoy the molds in blue cheese, soy sauce, miso, and many cured foods. Over generations, humans have essentially domesticated these molds, breeding them for flavor and other culinary purposes. Outside your kitchen, there is a tiny group of molds worth worrying about. When competing for space on a host, some species will engage in chemical warfare— producing colorful pigments, strong aromas, and dangerous compounds called mycotoxins. For example, a small group of molds that can grow on crops like barley, wheat, corn, and peanuts can produce aflatoxin, which is known to cause liver and lung cancer. Fortunately, most countries perform rigorous food safety testing to ensure aflatoxin never reaches the public. Despite these malevolent mycotoxins, most of the molds you encounter aren’t something to fear. And with this mindset, your fridge might feel a little less frightening and a lot more... alive.

1qrGwX9kQoQ.tx: Earlier this year, a bunch of us on the team who make SciShow got together at a retreat in New Orleans. This is a real video, don’t worry. Stick with me. And some of us wanted to take in the local culture at Mahogany Jazz Hall. We were enthusiastically welcomed by a hostess named Lexi, who hooked us up with some delicious absinthe cocktails and told us a bunch of interesting stories about the science of absinthe. The next morning… after a couple glasses of water… we decided to dig further into the topic, and it was just as fascinating as she promised. Indeed, we uncovered a historical mystery. For decades, absinthe was outlawed across Europe and North America due to its supposed hallucinogenic properties. But thanks to some recent studies, the true source of its psychedelic reputation is beginning to emerge. Absinthe is a spirit flavored with a distinct combination of herbs, including anise and wormwood. Wormwood has medicinal properties – it’s useful against, well, worms. These properties were known to the ancient Greeks, Romans, and Egyptians. But it’s much more recently that someone had the idea of putting it in cocktails. Absinthe was first industrially produced at the end of the 18th century, and all through the 19th, it was incredibly popular. It was given a lift by a failed wine grape harvest in France, but by 1900 or so, everybody was drinking it. Vincent van Gogh, Oscar Wilde, Ernest Hemingway, Aleister Crowley… And because we know the movies would never lie to us, it doesn’t just get you drunk. The so-called “Green Fairy” makes you see things. I mean, we’ve all watched Moulin Rouge!… …What? Nicole Kidman? Ewan McGregor? Get on that! In the latter half of the 19th century, doctors began to characterize a condition they called absinthism, in which chronic consumption of absinthe was associated with hallucinations, convulsions, speech impairment, and even death. Much of this came from the work of a French physician named Valentin Magnan. And even by 19th century standards, his research methods weren’t amazing. He used wormwood essence rather than absinthe in his experiments, for one thing. He was even criticized in the pages of The Lancet, a prestigious medical journal that’s still around, in 1869. They pointed out that the symptoms he described couldn’t be distinguished from what we’d now call alcohol use disorder. Hold on to that thought. Nevertheless, this concept of absinthism gained traction, and got caught up in the larger temperance movement at the beginning of the 20th century. Absinthe was banned in the United States in 1912, as something of a dry run for Prohibition. Several European states outlawed absinthe starting in 1905, and France, although its people were consuming sixty liters of absinthe per person per year, joined the banned wagon in 1915. This year is usually seen as the official start of the absinthe ban. Having vanquished the Green Fairy and its evils for good, scientists turned to the question of what could have caused the terrible symptoms of absinthism. And for a while, they thought they had it. Wormwood contains a neurotoxic chemical called thujone. Thujone blocks the activity of receptors that bind the neurotransmitter GABAA. This leads to convulsions, although the dose required isn’t totally clear. Thujone is also in sage, incidentally, and is a good reason to be careful around essential oils containing sage, since there’s way more of it there than in absinthe. As we’re fond of saying around here, the dose makes the poison. One study in 1999 estimated that pre-ban absinthe could have contained up to 260 milligrams of thujone per liter, way above what we’d now consider safe. However… we’ll be revisiting this number later. For now, take it with a grain of salt. ...or cube of sugar? Anyway.
